Protect Thine Own
1 pool
Political Card - Worth 1 Vote. Called by any justicar or Inner Circle
member at +1 stealth. Choose a non-Camarilla, non-titled vampire with
a capacity below 6. If the acting vampire is a member of the Inner
Circle, you may choose any non-Camarilla vampire instead. If this
referendum is successful, burn that vampire. This acting vampire
cannot gain blood during this referendum.

3 minor changes, but it could have done with the first 2.
Make the vote cost a pool, not a blood.
Make the vampire targeted need to be younger. Not a big change, but
it means you can't nuke other players vote decks. And many big vamps
have incidental titles.
Make it impossible to voter cap.

> overpowered Powers, and endlessly multiplying convictions (this gave
> them too much resiliency, and slowed the game down excessively). I
> can't think of a "fix" that would have been simple and solved the

X Pool, where X is the number of other events in play.
Gehenna. Requires at least one other gehenna card in play. Each Imbued

requirements. An imbued that performs a successful action may gain 1
conviction from his or her ash heap. An Imbued can only gain 1

now.

PTO was fine. It's not as though the Camarilla were ripping it up on
the tourney scene. Sure it was a bummer to have your 10 pointer burned
across table without much recourse. I'd say it's more of a bummer [and
far more common] getting bled for 15 odd pool on the second turn of

The Imbued do not slow the game down. Bad players slow the game down.
It takes all of two seconds to fish a burned conviction from your ash
pile after a succesful action. If recouping convictions was leading to
slowed down games, your Imbued players are bad. Sorry.

Of all the complaints against the Imbued I ever ever saw, none of the
were directed at Edge Explosion. This ban has come totally out of the
blue.

> Memories of Mortality could have possibly done with just turning it
> unique, I will admit, but errata is messy, and the fact that it can be
> recycled with Anthelios (the only card on my hate list that is still
> legal) / Parthenon meant that it might not have been a suitable fix.

I'm fortunate enough to have been playing this game long enough to

feel sorry for the guys who paid premium prices on ebay for cards that

Edge Explosion shows a potential problem of being able to create a
pretty strong card and then have it turn up on every Imbued in a deck -
Champion being an obvious example - which allows the deck to do
something it wouldn't ordinarily be able to do. So power cards could
lead to relatively homogenized decks - none of them are identical, but
they often share a similar core.

One positive flipside of this is that it might allow LSJ to create more
Powers that are similarly good, but which are restricted to only the
Imbued with the relevant Virtue. i.e. since it can only be played by a
small number of Imbued in a group pair (assuming new Imbued are
printed), there's less worry about being able to create a deck where all

But the above is not true:

A -> B -> C -> D -> E ->

B (who was first seed) ousts C and D.

A -> B(2) -> E ->

A now ousts B.

A(1) -> E ->

E can no longer win the game, though she is still playing.

If A ousts E, she will take first with 3 VP. If E ousts A, however,
she will lose the two-way 2 VP tie with the already ousted B, who has
better placement.

In this case, E gets to choose who wins (well, sort of - clearly A is
not interested in rolling over), but cannot win herself. There are
presumably other, 1 VP, 'tiebreaker' cases.

>James Coupe wrote:

>> In earlier games, you might choose to come a reasonable second instead

Yes. They have two outcomes in the finals.

1) Come first.
2) Come second.

This is not like the preliminary rounds where risky strategies have
massive downsides. If the risks you take to come first don't work, you
come second. Just like they would anyway.

If there is even the tiniest chance of winning, the player should play
for it in the final. What happens if it doesn't work? They come
second. Just like when they self oust. So clearly, playing for the
tiny chance is the maximized outcome.

>> In the final, if you have *any* chance to come first, however tiny,
>> you play for it. What's the worst that can happen? You come second.
>> And if you're in a lost position, you come second anyway.
>
>This is pretty unaccurate,

No it's not. Either you come first by shooting for a really stupid,
unlikely option or, worst case scenario, you come second. Just like you
would have done. You're not punished for trying to come first and
failing. You just come second. Just like before.

>but you seem to miss the point.

No, I haven't.

>Players are expected to maximize their outcome, are they ?

Players must play to win. In the final, this means that if they have
even the tiniest chance of winning, they play for it, because they
*cannot* make their situation worse. Absolutely cannot.

If chance of winning = 1% and they play for it, 1% of the time they win.
If they self-oust, they come second. If they play for it and don't win,
they come second.

Thus, by the laws of not being an idiot, playing for the 1% chance is
playing to win. It is the maximized outcome.

>Now that there's no outcome in final but first place (all the rest tie for
>second) ,
> once a player will be in a lost position,

A lost position here would be absolutely *zero* chance of anything.
*Very* few players end up in that situation. They often end up in
unlikely situations, and in preliminary rounds they may then choose to
play for a safe second, or make a deal to come second, or whatever.

Not relevant here. If they have even the slightest chance of winning,
play for it. Even if it's 0.0001%. Play for it. It CANNOT make your
situation worse, because you'll come second no matter what. If it
works, you come first.

>Before, giving up (self oust) would have result in non-maximizing a lost
>position (aming for 2,3,4 or place, or just securing the actual one),

And giving up here means that you lose even the slimmest chance of
winning the game. How is that playing to win? Can you win when you've
self ousted? No. Have you got even the tiniest chance in the world to
win? Play for it. If you hang on for two, three turns, is it possible
you'll have a tiny chance then? Then stick around for that!

Again, this isn't like the earlier rounds. You don't have anything to
lose. There's no comfortable second place to lose by exploding and
coming last on the table. You're going to come second come what may.
Take *ANY* chance you have. You don't have to judge whether it's
reasonable, likely, or plausible. If you stick around, you still have
the tiniest chance of winning.

In the old rules, all players in the final were assumed to be playing to
win/best outcome (including prize splits etc.), so we've monkeyed around
with assumptions in the final before. The monkeying around has changed.
In the new rules, even the slightest chance of winning is better than
not being in the final.

>So, again: why he/she should go on playing the final round at that point ?

Because trying for even the tiniest chance in the world of winning is
better than not winning.

By not being in the final, they can't win. By staying in the final, the
faintest chance of winning will still exist and the situation can
change. We must all have seen games where two players cross-table
suddenly fuck up and someone crawls back from absolutely nowhere at all,
and goes on to win. Unlikely, implausible, stupid things do happen.

Taking an option that definitely leads to you coming second (and you
cannot do worse than second) when sticking around means there's a tiny
chance you might come first is clearly not playing to win.

James has already done an admirable job of trying to explain the very
straightforward mathematics of the risk analysis involved in the new
finals scheme vs. the old; it's entirely unclear to me what part of
his explanation you are missing, but still I'll try to add to it.

The first time I had a multiple choice test in elementary school, I
didn't answer some of the questions, because I didn't know the
answer. When I showed the test to my father, he pointed out that this
was not a good strategy - since there was no penalty for guessing, you
should always pick some one of the choices, on the off chance that you
get it right. (And if you can narrow down the choices, you increase
your chances.) Not answering guarantees getting it wrong.

So it will be with finals: you should never self-oust*, as you are
guaranteeing that you will come in second, whereas if you stay in the
game you will always have some chance, however small, of coming in
first.

*Unless you mathematically have 0% chance of winning, which is
possible, as I demonstrated elsewhere in this thread. Possible, but
presumably rare and unlikely. And even in the case I posited, the
player with a 0% chance of winning still had influence over who won!

Now, you're confusing me, in turn. I'm guessing the disconnect is
semantic: either a difference in what each of means by "personality"
or perhaps that I'm talking about deck archetypes (in truth) where
you're talking the personality of each player's individual implementation
of an Imbued deck.

Take Champion, for example. It is a power card requiring the virtue
of Defense. Under the current rules, which allow Edge Explosion,
Champion can potentially be played on any Imbued. And since almost
all Imbued decks will include an Edge Explosion, chances are that
decks using Champion will use a number of Imbued who do not have
defense, selected for their individual power (card text, such as
Jennifer Orne's critical change to the rules applying to Imbued
leaving the incapacitated region) or higher degree of conformance
to a more critical/immediately needed virtue in the deck. Arbitrary
combinations of cards requiring various virtues are much easier.
Since such arbitrary combinations of virtues are much more possible
given the use of Edge Explosion, it's true that individual decks
will tend to have much more "personality". But the massed effect
of not requiring players to make hard decisions such as the need
to choose more Imbued for their possession of the Defense virtue
is to muddy the whole field of Imbued decks. That is, there aren't
distinct *types* of decks which emerge based on things like a
dearth of good Imbued which contain two particular virtues that
players might otherwise like to combine. Jennifer Orne may not
be in every Imbued deck because some players, trying to do
some very distinct thing with virtues, will find there's no room
for her in their crypt. This, hopefully, will give rise to more
distinctly discernable Imbued deck archetypes.

> somehow going to increase the variety of cards played,

to play them to be competitive, that might decrease the variety
of cards played since it would decrease the variety in viable decks.
In that sense, Edge Explosion might increase the variety in cards
played because people will feel freer to play something else besides
Imbued, animalism intercept/combat, and the few other things that
have a reasonable chance at ousting Imbued decks. But that's a whole
other argument and I wasn't talking about it. I actually just said
it would increase the personality of Imbued decks - by which I meant
one should see Imbued deck archetypes becoming more distinct and
classifiable due to having to specialize more.

Fred

> Banning EE isn't going to give us a greater variety of imbued decks,
> because it's not really possible to build, say, a mono-Vengeance deck
> that's substantially different from a mono-Vision deck. There just
> aren't enough cards available to each virtue to make a huge difference
> possible (even setting aside the issue of the many imbued cards which
> just aren't worth playing, which is a very real issue).

Why do we need lots of different cards available? I don't get that.
As long as there are different & useful cards available, that will
create the increased distinctness in different kinds of Imbued decks.
Again, returning to the example of Champions. In 2008, you'll be
much less able to just throw some Champions into any 'ol Imbued deck
as is generally done now and expect Edge Explosion to cover you even
if you chose few Imbued with Defense. You'll have to think about
which Imbued you use in your crypt and how many Champions that crypt
can support. If you find you can't support many or even any Champions,
you'll have to look at how the relative lessening of your defensive
capabilities might need to be covered. By throwing in more reaction
cards? More bloat to cover the pool you expect to lose because you're
blocking fewer bleeds? Whatever it is, it will become distinctly
associated with the type of deck you're building. The days of having
so many ways to cover everything with precisely the Imbued you want
in your deck are gone. Options are narrowed and deckbuilders will have
to rely more on disciplined choices, which in turn will create distinct
definition in terms of cards and crypt members chosen for separate
types of Imbued decks.

I'm not sure why you think it takes a lot card types for a given
virtue to create that distinction. It doesn't take a lot of different
Thaumaturgy cards to create a Cryptic Mission deck and it's one of the
most distinctive decks out there.

> What we'll get
> instead is imbued decks which are mostly the same as each other but
> with a few variations based on available virtues.

It sounds like you anticipate Imbued decks powered almost completely
through use of their conviction cards using the conviction card text
functions and non-Imbued decks and not using their power cards hardly at
all. Maybe, but I doubt it. Power cards are just too powerful to
ignore just because you won't have the opportunity to put any power
card you want on any Imbued you want. I think Power cards will still
make up the core of most Imbued decks and the virtue specialization
that will now be forced on Imbued players will insure distinctiveness.

> As a thought experiment, consider four hypothetical vampire clans
> which each only have access to eight different discipline cards. How
> different are monoclan decks based around those clans going to be from
> each other? Not very, since the bulk of their library will be based
> mainly on disciplineless cards, which have the same availability to
> all those clans.

Here again, your proximate conclusion about the predominance of
disciplineless cards is not the one I'd come to, hence I don't come to
the same final conclusion. I think the monoclan decks would be quite
different from one another - but it depends on which discipline cards
the various clans were left with. If they were relatively narrow and/or
ineffective cards, you'd be right. I don't think Imbued power cards are
either.

>> I actually just said
>> it would increase the personality of Imbued decks - by which I meant
>> one should see Imbued deck archetypes becoming more distinct and
>> classifiable due to having to specialize more.
>
> I think we're going to see imbued decks based even more around the
> specials on the crypt cards than we used to, which will lead to even
> more homogeneity among imbued decks. I'd be very happy to be proven
> wrong about this, and even happier if more imbued cards were printed
> (which would lead to less of that homogeneity).

I think if you get proven right about the former, the latter may well
happen. If that proves to be the case, although I'd be sorry that Imbued
would have to suffer a kind of interregnum of boring ineffectiveness and
irrelevance before being made interesting again, I still think it's
better than the existing state of affairs. And it would allow the
designers to put more thought into what role Imbued should actually play
in this game with the hindsight of some real experience. I might even
come to enjoy their contribution to the game some day.

Fred

extent (some are there for defense, some for bloat, some for other
things, etc.) and aren't the multifunction things they are now - once
EE gets on the board. And you maybe look for three or four virtues
to use and the Imbued which can supply two of them become mainstays

provide useful interactions with the virtue-based cards and which
cover for the virtues you no longer have access to. I would think
it would be more than "a bit".

range of virtue cards would make it more possible but it's not
necessary.

I'm actually wondering what players will come up with they're forced
to look a lot harder. Before, it wasn't very hard to create something
effective so I imagine players poured a little of this and a little of
that to taste, depending on their playstyle. Now that it's going to be
a lot harder to cover all the bases, deckbuilders will be forced to
become innovative. Of course, "fun decks" are what you get when people
searching for answers just aren't finding them, either because they
haven't looked hard enough for the answers or the answers just aren't
out there (could be either thing). You may be right in the end - in
which case one would expect stuff to eventually get re-added back in,
perhaps the reappearance of scaled back Edge Explosion, MoM, or perhaps
new cards or who knows? But I wouldn't be surprised if you were wrong.

Fred

I would love to be wrong. But I don't think I am (wall of text
warning):

There are 6 minions in the game with Defense. Judgment is shared by
two of them. There are 3 cards that require defense (Rejuvenate,
Champion, and Lock), and one that requires a defender (Vigil). Vigil
is okay, but it can only give intercept to one of three Defenders.
Rejuvenate and Champion are decent, but only because they untap you
when you get them. Lock is decent, when you back it up with a bucket
full of table hate - by which I mean Society of Leopold, Vampiric
Disease, and Gehenna Events. You can splash some Vigilance or Discern
- and you'll need to. Chances are good that after playing this deck,
you'll decide that Vigilance is the best card in it, break it down,
and make a Judgment deck that splashes Defense instead.

There are 8 (!) minions with Innocence. One of them is Beatrice, who
may or may not fit into your deck. Of these, 2 have judgment, 2 have
redemption, and 2 have vision. Innocents have access to Inspire,
Illuminate, Hide, and Bond. Bond isn't great, especially given that
Jennie's got innocence, so you've got your leave-incapacited route
halfway covered already. Illuminate is wallpapered by The Unmasking.
Hide is great for keeping Jennie from being rushed, but not so much
for anything else. Inspire is good enough to build a deck around. And
you can even splash Judgment, Vision, or Redemption. Judgment and/or
Vision likely win, because a) Jennie has both of them, and she's worth
including multiple copies of anyway, and b) Redemption largely sucks.
Alternatively, you can keep splashing to a minimum and just try to put
your entire crypt into play. Innocence probably does fine, IF the EE
ban reduces general anti-imbued table hate enough. Because putting 5+
minions in play attracts enough hate when they aren't imbued. Note
that I built decks like this pre-ban, and thought they were fine, but
never played them because they're swarm-breed decks, and vampires can
typically do it better (also, Inspire is rare).

There are 7 minions with Judgment. One of them is Earl Deams, who
burns a conviction each turn if you have more than 2 imbued, but he
also gets +1 stealth, so he's worth it at least sometimes. Of the 7, 2
have defense, 2 have innocence, and 2 have vision (Earl is one of the
ones with Vision, though, so it's hard to splash anything worthwhile -
he won't have the conviction to pay for it). Vigilance and Discern are
awesome. Imprison costs too much conviction to ever be played and
Antithesis has to many target restrictions to be worth packing more
than a prayer copy or two. You get to use Darby Dance tech. You can
splash some Champion, which is probably necessary. And you're good to
go.

There are 5 minions with Martyrdom. Two of them have vision. One of
them is Earl Deams, who burns a conviction every turn. Two of them
(Anna Suljic and Earl Deams) cost 6 pool each. Martyrdom has access to
Inflict, Donate, Project, and Expiate. Expiate and Inflict are junk.
Earl will be deadweight in this deck because everything costs
conviction. So you have 4 crypt choices available. Donate's pretty
solid, when you have the conviction to pay for it, which was already
somewhat difficult to manage with EE refueling it every turn, and will
now be even harder. You can't afford to splash vision, because Earl is
one of the two minions you have with Vision, and he's dead weight. No
other virtue is shared by even 2 of your crypt choices. You have no
access to untap outside of Angel of Berlin and

There are 5 minions with Redemption. 2 of these have innocence, and 2
have vision. One of these is Anna Suljic, who costs 6 pool. The cards
available to redemption are Respire, Shame, Punish, and Abjure.
Respire's target restriction and lack of stealth makes it weak without
Wormwood and a ton of Gehenna events to back it up. Shame's target
restrictions and high conviction cost make it weak. Punish is just
weak. Abjure is interesting in a post-EE world, because it's another
way to reliably gain conviction. However, it only gains conviction for
a minion with Redemption, so I'm not convinced it's worthwhile. You
can splash vision for Determine if you want, or Innocence for Inspire.
When you're done, you're still going to have a ridiculously hard time
going forward because you've got no true wake-up ability.

There are 6 minions with Vengeance. None of these minions share any
other virtues. One of these minions is Beatrice Tremblay, who is bad
news in a vengeance deck. Vengeance has access to Muse of Flame,
Cleave, Smite, and Surge. Muse of Flame's only real uses came from the
fact that it is at +2 stealth and therefore unlikely to get blocked.
Once upon a time, this could trigger both conviction gain from EE and
untap via Vigilance for multi-rush. The first is now impossible, and
the second is only usable by John O'Malley. Cleave is a poor
substitute for Increased Strength (inferior) and Smite is an
overcosted Taste of Death. Surge is nice, but one of the key minions
in a Vengeance deck, Jennifer Vidisania, has -1 stealth and is
therefore unlikely to ever be able to get it. Avengers have access to
Living Wood Staff, which is nice, but you're usually better off just
using more Weighted Walking Sticks instead. The only thing Vengeance
really has going for it is that you can play Tension and Dragonbound
without them coming back to bite you. However, you don't have access
to many of the kinds of cards like Taste and Grapple that, as Peter
Bakija has repeatedly put it, make combat decks go. Vengeance is a lot
like Quietus-lite, and not worth pursuing seriously.

There are 6 minions with Vision. 2 each have Innocence, Judgment,
Martyrdom, and Redemption. One of these minions is Earl Deams. Another
is Anna Suljic. Vision has access to Augur, Foresee, and Determine.
Visionaries have access to Unity. Unity is good for recycling
Determine, but costs pool to use and Visionaries aren't good at
recouping that pool. Augur is decent because it untaps you, but costs
a conviction and you don't have much to back it up with. Foresee isn't
very good - if you want to end combat, use a Flash Grenade, if you
want to look at someone's hand, use Augur. Vision doesn't let you
splash much in the way of Martyrdom, because of Earl's Drawback.
Judgment splashes okay for some Vigilance and/or Discern, because
Jennie's always good, and Earl's drawback is outweight by the fact
that he gets either power at an extra +1 stealth. Redemption might be
worth splashing for Abjure, both to protect Jennie and to recoup some
conviction. Innocence can splash some Inspire as usual. If you don't
own an Unmasking, you can also recycle Illuminate with Unity to get a
similar, though much more expensive effect.

You can, of course, do more than splashing two virtues - you can split
your crypt. But one of the virtues is nearly always going to have to
be Judgment, unless you're going with Innocence as your primary,
because you either need the untap from Vigilance or the Swarm/Bloat
tech if you're going to have a chance of surviving while you go
forward. If you're using Judgment anyway, you're typically going to be
better off switching to mainly Judgment and splashing some other stuff
so that you can make better use of Darby Dance tech.

The other option is to use Flash Grenades to limit your need for untap
and Travis to cover your bloat angle, going (nearly) powerless. Once
you've made that decision, you're better off just forgoing the powers
entirely and packing more Flash Grenades, and now we actually _are_
picking our minions just for their specials and not for their virtues.

-witness1

On Dec 7, 1:47 am, "Frederick Scott" <nos...@no.spam.dot.com> wrote:

Wow, I have no idea how to even begin responding to that. Do you
think that's actually how anyone builds a decent Imbued deck in 2007?
'Cause it smells like a straw man to me - it's certainly not something
I'd have done, or saw done. Edge Explosion just didn't allow the sort
of willy-nilly "toss it in" add-ons you're implying it did.

Had you said Vigilance, you *might* have had a point - that's a card
worth getting on any and every Imbued you can, and thus, at least for
me, was the one I assumed my Edge Explosion would help me wedge onto
the support Imbued I was running that didn't have Judgment to begin
with. But even then, the deck had to function before EE came out, so
I wasn't relying on it to let me play one of the few powers worth
mentioning.

Edge Explosion was all about the Convictions, which as others have
said is really the most important facet of an Imbued deck - see all
the Scrounging/Liquidation/Specialization tech that goes into decks to
get them in the discard pile fast and at a profit. Edge Explosion was
in my decks almost solely because it allowed faster recovery of
convictions, so that I could do something more often than once every
third or so turn, and so that the powers, reactions, and other cards
that cost conviction were worth using. Inspire is barely worthwhile
at 1 conviction for 1 bloat down, and it means that particular
Innocent is basically just an Ecoterrorists that can be blocked,
'cause she's not doing anything else when every turn's conviction
powers the Inspire and that's all. If I've got to blow a Second Sight
to get an Inspire action through (which, typically, is a decent plan),
that means it's costing 2 conviction, effectively, which means it's
not quite worth it. Recovering those conviction with EE, so that you
could make progress rather than maintain state if nothing went wrong,
was fairly critical.

I'll grant that it was Edge Explosion that made Champion viable as a
defense mechanism, but it wasn't because it let you put it on anyone
willy-nilly. It was because it let you regain the hefty two
conviction cost most turns, provided you had a vigilance to end up
untapped with and a successful action to take to get that second one
back and untap...

- D.J.

This is true to vampire-based decks because no matter how good a card
such as, say, Freak Drive is, there are tons of other good cards that
require other Disciplines and clans and titles and such. The Imbued
simply don't have that. That's why numbers are important here - not
because a limited pool of cards strangle creativity *in principle*,
but because *in this particular case* the pool is *too* small. 14
Powers, 3 creed-requiring cards and 4 cards any Imbued can use (not
taking EE into account anymore). Even if all of them were as good as,
say, Freak Drive, it would be hard to come up with more than a few
deck archetypes out of them.

You simply don't have anywhere to run unless you treat an Imbued deck
as an Ally Deck With Convictions and forget the Powers. Sure, this
sounds like it's doable since there are so many ally decks around -
except that these allies usually are supported by vampires, a thing
that seems difficult to do with the Imbued since they don't interact
that well unless you're using one or two lone Imbued in a vampire-
based deck for their specials. Just check the NoR cards. There's
Respire and Rejuvenate, which give a vampire or ally a whooping 1
blood/life, costing 1 conviction. There's Anna Suljic's and Mama
Boumba's specials, which are neat for a vampire-based deck but nothing
that vampire-based cards can't do (and better, depending on the clan/
disciplines you're using). You can always use a Vision-enabled Imbued
to give Determine to a clan-based deck with no readily available
bounce, but then again you could do it with few dom weenies and some
DIs, and maybe even get some Discipline synergy in the process. And
most of the Discipline- or clan-based cards that help allies either
don't work with the Imbued or do not offer any effect that, say,
Respire or Rejuvenate or a Jacket won't do, and then you don't run the
risk of clogging your hand with cards your Imbued can't play. What
else?

We need to wait to see how things go in the long run, but for what
I've seen it still seems we'll see less Imbued deck archetypes, not
more. At least not competitive ones, and at least not until we get a
few more Powers that combo well with the less used ones already
released. A few players will try to get the most out of 3 or 4 Powers/
Imbued cards they never used before, but that'll have minimal impact.
My prediction for now is that Imbued wall decks based on Vigilance and
Imbued swarm based on Flash Grenade will boom.

Making a (probably bad) analogy, imagine how well the Ravnos would do
just after Dark Sovereigns was released if, say, Sensory Deprivation
or Fata Morgana had been banned then. I'd guess it wouldn't make
people start to create new deck archetypes based on that clan just
because one viable card was wiped out, at least not until Final Nights
came by. It would just kill one of the few (more or less) viable deck
archetypes for the Ravnos at the time.
And in this hypothetical situation, at least some Ravnos had
Discipline synergy with other clans, mainly the Gangrel. The Imbued
simply don't. They're on their own.

> Cool. You may be right that powers need Edge Explosion to be useful
> enough to bother with other than, say, just concentrating on Judgement
> and splashing Defense. Still, attempting to play the real game in
> the real world may uncover more ways of using specific _other_ powers

I'd love to see that happen. Except that it seems unlikely right now -
some Imbued players have tried it before, and usually what you'll see
is new equipments being incorporated, maybe one or other
disciplineless combat cards or a new Master such as Therbold Realty or
King's Rising and that's all. Even then they're iffy - no one would
ever use them casually in a vampire-based deck since there are better
options - and none of those cards are really prone to combo with the
Powers in any integral way.

When I got away from the game for a while, earlier this year, this was
one of the issues that were bugging me about the Imbued. I wanted to
make Imbued-based decks with a splash of something else, something
unexpected, made out of a couple vampires added to the crypt and/or a
combo with old, regular cards, and see how it goes. It was difficult.
One of the few ideas I had that *seemed* viable enough to give it a
try was to use merged Alan Sovereign in a Defense/Judgment wall deck
with guns - so to get mileage out of Investments, pay less for the
guns and splash in a few Deflections. Didn't work as well as the pure
Imbued deck using virtually the same tech; the Alan-based module
simply hampered the deck's flow too much.

> If not, then the problem is total lameness is
> some of the virtues - which I wasn't accounting for when I made the
> claim.
> Fred

I wouldn't say total lameness is to blame, though some Virtues do
merit that designation. It's more like... How the Imbued don't mesh
well with vampires and vampire-based cards, including most 'normal'
allies. Of course, the overall theme of NoR lends naturally to this,
but in terms of variety, this limits the deckbuilding options, EE/MoM
banned or not.
So far, it seems getting EE banned doesn't really diminishes overall
power level equally across the Imbued field, just eliminates a number
of deck possibilities and leaves a void to be filled later.

Two players - let's say, you and me - are sat on a table. I'm in a
really shitty position. I'm obviously going to play to win, but things
are really bad for some reason. I don't have a great deal of likelihood
of going anywhere without some help. You, on the other hand, can
probably get a VP or maybe two, but if you can keep me on the table, you
think you can get the win.

Now, assume we're playing on a preliminary table - normal rules, game
wins, VPs matter etc. I might be able to hang on for 0.5VP, I might
get ousted, it's pretty seriously unlikely I'll get a VP on my own. You
say "Hey, I've got this really neat idea. How about we..." and you come
up with a VP split deal. Do I take it or don't I? Maybe I don't think
it's good enough, maybe I don't think it will work, maybe I don't like
VP split deals, maybe you pissed me off in an earlier round by burning
Saulot and I hate you for it. But, suppose I take it. Is it in my
interests? Yes, if it works. And we (you, me, the table, the judge
etc.) judge it to be a good risk if someone quibbles. Is it a good deal
for you? Sure it is! You've gone from 1 or 2 VPs to a pretty good
chance of a table-win.

Now repeat in the final. I'm pretty certain that I can't go anywhere
too well. Under the new rules, I'm still going to play for first
because it can't hurt me.

Let's say that the prize is something like 10 boosters each for the
second place people, and more boosters, a trophy, a piece of artwork,
and bragging rights for the winner - you've just become the LSJLand
Continental Champion, after all.

Specifically, in the new rules, I have no reason to help you secure a
game win. Short term deals? Absolutely. I'll rescue your Nergal to
stop him being eaten if you lend me some votes with Ferraile, for
example. Medium term deals? Probably. Man, it's some cocktastic Legacy
of Pander deck that's going to roll the table. Kill it. Then we'll
fight it out like men. Long-term VP split deals? Not in my interest
really. I have no interest (from the game) in helping you win. I mean,
you might be my mate, and we can't do a lot about that in the rules
structure, but you can't give me your prizes, you can't bribe me with
stuff, you're the one with the bragging rights and your name on the
trophy. I have no incentive not to try to win myself. I'll get 10
boosters anyway.

But go back to the preliminary stages, and think "Why would I give up my
chance to win to come second?" Well, it's a better outcome for me than
I reasonably expected otherwise. So I was happy with the 2 VP you let
me have, and you were happy with the table win you secured.

Now, the final. I will get 10 boosters anyway. Reasonably, I don't
think I can do massively better than joint 2nd. Someone else is just
too good for me, the nemesis to my deck, whatever. Now, using exactly
the same deal as we used above in the preliminary round, I don't think I
stand a reasonable chance of winning. Very unlikely, sure. But if I
think that I'm going to get 10 boosters and go home, or I could play for
the reasonable chance of 20 boosters (10 + 2*5, say), you're going to
have players who are willing to do that.

In the old (current) version, we already had players who were willing to
negotiate to get second place, if it meant that they did better than
they thought they would. And there would be many people who might make
that deal from your side, too - you get 3VP, a game win, 25 boosters
(10+5*3), bragging rights, trophy, artwork. Yeah, 35 boosters would be
hot, but this way you secure the game win. And you needed my help to do
that in a reasonable way. So you get all the cool stuff, I get 20
boosters, everyone else gets 10.

There will be many players who'd make such a deal, if they thought they
were going to go home with less. Would you? Would I? Maybe, maybe
not. Would other people? I'd be willing to bet money on it that it
would happen.

If I think I have a one in a million shot at winning, because if you

OK, here is where you need to look a little harder at what I'm saying.
Your comments seem to indicate that you're missing my point or
deliberately ignoring it or some such. You do have to accept a few
obvious assumptions and one of them is admittedly attackable in the
current environment: that one could build a solid deck from a single
vampire's virtues. If you accepted that for the sake of argument, you
should be able to understand why removing Edge Explosion - which everyone
would normally mindlessly always throw in all Imbued decks, I think
(extreme corner case situations notwithstanding) - would force Imbued
deckbuilders to make decisions that hadn't been forced to make before.
Before you could have your Champions AND your Vigilances. Now you have
to decide which of the two you want or alternative if you want to make
a stab at creating an awkward deck which uses both, albeit usually not
on the same Imbued.

The requirement that deckbuilders be forced to make such decisions
between various paths to victory is a good thing and certainly one of
the charms of collectible card games. And it may be a reality of
Imbued decks in the future if it isn't now.

> We looked at the cards NoR offers, tried, and made decisions based on
> how useful they were! Why do you think the decision tree is magically
> larger now that EE is banned?

It's hard to say. Perhaps not but that's beside the point. You speak
as if a decision tree cannot become larger as a result of the removal
of a card and this is certainly not true. Consider some overpowered card
requiring an 11-cap Ravnos to play it as an action which almost always
led the player who played it to victory. Because it's so overpowered and
easy to play, decks including the card and whatever is needed to
successfully play it (e.g. Hazimel or Ezmerelda plus supporting 10-caps
with discipline cards, action modifiers which make actions unblockable)
and probably throwing in things which would prevent others from
successfully playing it (e.g. Direct Interventions, Rewind Time) would
dominate. The decision tree would become very small. Remove the card
and the decision tree magically becomes larger.

> Do you really think all of us have
> blinders on? That we can't try things or leave the beaten path?
> That's what it sounds like and it's frankly a little insulting.

I don't know why you think it's insulting. Sure, you can try crazy
things like sticking to a single virtue in the power cards you choose
and basing decks around the single virtue - but why would you as long
as there's Edge Explosion? So pardon me if I suspect that although
you may have tried something more or less like this, you may not have
tried it very hard because there was no reason to. It may be fair to
say it's not _worth_ trying given what you can see is out there. But
whatever the case, allow me a few doubts that people may not have tried
it all that exhaustively prior to this banning.

> I've left Theory Land, come
> join me in Reality Land. The cards that exist, now, for reals, are
> inadequate for building a variety of decks based on all the virtues.
> You get 3, maybe 4 virtues that are good as printed, right now. In
> theory, you are right. But we're not talking in abstractions.

All right, fair enough. But don't forget, theory land may also become
future land at some point - with more cards.

Fred

This is generally true, but the problem I see in your assertion from
the very beginning is that EE doesn't really qualify for that
comparison because it wasn't really the cause for that situation to
form in certain playgroups. The Imbued - and how they easily fit with
playing many Events - *as a whole* may qualify, but EE played no real
part in it, not specifically. I mean, EE is neither the main reason
why people play Imbued nor the main target for anti-Imbued tech, like
it would happen with your theoretical overpowered card requiring
Ezmerelda/Hazimel.

I'll insist on it: what can the Imbued players can 'focus on' now that
they can't use EE? Really, where are the ideas? Where are the new
branches of the decision tree - or rather, to which direction can
these branches really grow?

All EE did was to accelerate the regaining of Convictions and let
deckbuilders include a couple or so crypt choices they wouldn't
otherwise, and even then such deckbuilders would add a bit of setup to
make it work properly (Forttschrit Library or whatever). Even then the
card wasn't being used in multiples for the very obvious reason that
it's an event. Having to get rid of those 2-4 library cards that
comprise the 'EE module', or to swap a couple or so crypt choices,
won't change the decks people make, or the reactions the non-Imbued
players will have to those decks. Most, if not all, such decks will
just keep on doing what they already did, just with two more copies
of, say, certain Convictions or Powers they already had, or a couple
disciplineless Dodges/maneuvers, and swapping Travis for one more copy
of other Imbued the crypt already featured. Some decks will even keep
Jennie around, no matter if she can't play Champion or whatever
anymore in the mid/late game under EE - she's still worth it even if
you use only one of her Virtues in the deck. And the vampire-based
deck builders will still pack anti-Event and anti-ally tech as normal
to deal with the Imbued, which will still be played.

Not enough of a ripple effect to produce 'more distinct' decks.
They'll be the same at their cores. At most they'll become a lot more
focused, as spare copies of cards such as, say, Inflict (cost: 2
convictions) will be tossed out for extra copies of whatever is
essential to that deck using Martyrdom (namely, Donate) since now
these spare cards became too expensive to use even as prayer cards.
There's no real alternative to replacing those spare cards that will
make them more distinct, no matter how many disciplineless cards we
have in the game - since most of them aren't usable by allies anyway.
This will make good Imbued deck archetypes even more 'annoying',
because they'll be more thorough at what they do, just with a little
slower build-up. Just wait and see.

It's not like decks using a couple of copies of, say, Hungry Coyote
and Infernal Familiar (and maybe Spirit Summoning Chamber to get the
Familiar quicker) are that overpowered to the point everyone is
playing !Tremere and/or packing extra Sudden Reversal, Wash or
retainer-killing effects.

On one thing you're right: this has much more to do with how a number
of Powers and Imbued-based cards are crappy, and how some Virtues have
virtually nothing to offer (and I'd include some crypt specials too).
But it still means banning EE won't change the usual deckbuilding
parameters for those using Imbued, at least not until we get more
cards for the Imbued, if ever.

Fabio 'Sooner' Macedo

unavoidable until something new is brought into the equation - not an

Ravnos players stray away from other deck possibilities and opponent
players to include tech against it being played. Given the situation,

card and I couldn't. Ravnos players have competitive options, and if
they're not playing them because the theoretical card it's *so
powerful* then banning it will work to increase diversity. Imbued
players do not have much options that work in the first place, they're
already playing those options no matter if a couple of copies of EE

diversity field.

> In my mind, I think you minimize the value of Edge Explosion allowing

Which is probably the core of our disagreement: I think you
*overestimate* the value of that allowance, or even that it's really
viable as an integral part of an Imbued deck.

In my experience - and I admit it's not an indication on how things go
around the world, but I've seen no indication otherwise considering
decks posted in this board and in the TWDA - no single Imbued deck
really invested too much in making sure EE is in play before the
midgame, so to 'play powers in the order they come up'. Usually, it
was just better to keep it as a side module (2-3 EEs, 2 Fortschritt at
most) so to make it even more worthwhile to throw Travis or Jennie
into a crypt thanks to their specials (which will continue to be true,
it's just that you can't toss one or two EEs and make them even
*better* for the deck at some point, even if it only near the
endgame). Other decks just had one or two EE to make the deck fare
even better by gaining extra Convictions at some point in the game -
it simply didn't hurt.

This whole idea that people *could* just choose whenever Imbued they
feel like, ignore the Virtues for the most part, and toss in
Champions, Vigilances, Donates and EEs is, pardon the bluntness,
*alien* to me. Never seen it, and doesn't sound like an even remotely
good plan. Sounds like taking the smallest !Tremere around no matter
the Disciplines, tossing in 3x Infernal Pacts and playing, say, 4x
Govern the Unaligned, 4x Lost in Crowds, 4x Call of the Hungry Dead
and 4x Freak Drive thinking you're going to play all those latter 16
cards in the order they come. Not really feasible.

I know it's one more analogy with vampires, but the essential thing to
notice here is this: people already chose the Virtues they wanted when
building crypts, no matter the existence of EE, and still used the
same parameters vampire decks use - you need enough cards in the crypt
that possess the requirements to play the cards the library has, or
your hand will clog all the time, EE or not EE. EE just compensated
for the fact that there are way less crypt cards that fulfill the
requirement than usual (even less then bloodlines had at their time of
inception, in certain Virtue cases), so you could round up the crypt
with a couple more Imbued and expect them to do at least one thing
besides spending Convictions and activating their specials. Removing
EE will change nothing in the bigger picture where diversity is
concerned because of this. The only thing it will accomplish is to
make Travis or Jenni be slightly less used and the decks to
concentrate in an even smaller pool of worthwhile Powers, therefore
turning them even more alike.

> As we keep finding out, the Imbued/Vampire analogies are really
> treacherous because the two crypt card types have so many inherent
> differences in what you can do with them.

True, but then, when you outline a situation such as the 11-cap Ravnos
card, you're falling on the same trap. It's hard to avoid. But there's
a thing to consider: almost any regular, vampire-requiring card in the
game, no matter how *bad* it is, can shine if used in the right moment
and in the right combo because it *can* be combined with virtually
everything in the game. It may need an insane (and not really that
worthwhile) setup, but it can be done. Convictions and Powers aren't
really that flexible where combining is concerned (Convictions and a
couple of Powers, like Donate, are flexible on their own, of course).
They stand on their own for the most part, and when they combine with
something, it's with a fraction of the disciplineless library cards
(mainly masters, equipments and combat cards that have no requirements
or blood cost).

So if you remove from a given deck a card that allows playing a couple
or so extra Powers but doesn't give more options (either new Powers or
disciplineless cards) to fill that void, how do you achieve more
diversity in deckbuilding using Virtues? You don't. Because no one's
is letting this or that Power, or this or that disciplineless Dodge,
or this or that master out of the deck because of EE. Removing EE from
the equation doesn't make, say, Backstep or Haymaker a better choice
to Imbued decks.

But to take it for what it's
> worth, what I just heard you say is that Edge Explosion isn't very
> important to Imbued decks at all. I'm not sure that's what you meant
> but that's what the analogy parses down to. If EE isn't that important,
> then by extension, Imbued players shouldn't be affected by it that much
> or miss the card very much. Really?

Right now I'm limiting myself here to the issue at hand, which is
deckbuilding diversity and how banning EE relates to it.

I have 3 copies of EE and never used more than 2 in the same deck, and
that was only once. I played Imbued for months before I even *had* a
single copy of it, and my decks neither changed much after that nor
started to win more games. I do think EE is not important to the
*power levels* the Imbued can achieve. I do think, though, that
removing it will do nothing to increase diversity.

> Whatever the case, the flip side of your point - about players playing

In fact, it's not that the point ignores the fact that Events are
inherently difficult to prevent or remove - that fact is indeed an
integral part of the point. The ban on EE is like dealing with a
gallon of dirty water by removing a pint of its contents and putting
it into a water-cleaning machine. You can drink the pint of water now
that it's clean, but the gallon is still infected and will remain so.
You can slow down a few Imbued decks by removing EE out of the
equation, but people will still build very similar decks since EE
wasn't integral to almost all of them, and the reaction will still be
generally the same, and things won't really change. If anything, it's
even one more reason to substitute EE for, say, another event such as
Recalled to the Founder or Anthelios or Thirst or whatever.

I'm pretty sure we get the point. The thing is, there are two serious
limitations on the cards that currently exist: some of the virtues
don't have cards solid enough to build around (Redemption), and some
of the virtues that do have good cards, don't have the crypt support
to back them up (Martyrdom).

EE, in this environment, alleviates both sides, by enabling you to use
the first set of virtues as support virtues while building primarily
around something else, and expanding your crypt options when building
around the second set of virtues. So some distinctive decks die out
with an EE ban, but none are really created.

Yes, all this falls by the wayside if (enough) more cards get printed
for the imbued. If that's the plan, the ban of EE is probably
necessary to open up the design space to give each virtue a little
something special.

> choose between the virtues when you can choose *all* the virtues?

A) Because you can't (EE only allows each minion to get one extra
power of a virtue he doesn't have) and B) because it's generally not
worth the cost to your deck. See below.

By far the more important factor in EE is the conviction gain.
Generally speaking, you need the powers, equipment, masters, etc. to
fall out of your hand ASAP so that you cycle into more conviction, The
Unmasking, and Edge Explosion (in that order of priority). In turn,
the Conviction flows out of your hand during untap, refilling your
hand with more powers, etc.

It of course does help to get an early EE (a lot), but it helps even
more, IME, to build your deck such that you don't need it to get the
ball rolling.



In general, if the special is all that tremendous, you'll pick them
anyway. Looking through the ITWDA, in most of the decks, less than 25%
of the cards require any virtue/creed at all, and not all of them are
powers (and thus subject to EE). Even though we could theoretically
throw in any of those powers we wanted, they are never worth it if 9
times out of 10 you have to draw EE (and another Gehenna event) first.

> Or they allow
> you to combine use of powers in ways that the crypt offerings
> wouldn't otherwise support. Whatever, it's silly to pretend this
> doesn't matter. No one's telling you Edge Explosion allows you
> to forget about the relationship. Only that it allows you a
> great deal more freedom than you'd otherwise have. And that
> freedom can be cashed in for power, I think.

Sure. See also any Donate deck ever made - EE is largely what made it
go (boy it was fun to see Jake Washington bleed for 5). But even with
EE those decks are harder to win with than a good Darby Dance deck,
which really doesn't need any off-virtue powers at all. Primarily
because, in the Darby Dance deck, nearly all of your minions can play
nearly all of your powers without needing EE at all.

Powers, in general are weak. This is largely a good thing, IMO,
because they're permanents acquired at +1 stealth that untap you after
acquisition. But it also makes your points about EE largely moot,
because whenever the crypt options support it, it's better (for a
variety of reasons) to make use minions that already have the virtues
even when you're trying to play the strong powers.

In short:
If the purpose of the EE ban was to make imbued decks weaker, it
succeeds.
If the purpose of the EE ban was to make people bitch less about the
imbued on the newsgroup, by God I hope it succeeds, and will count it
as a moral VP.
If the purpose of the EE ban was to open up the design space for
future imbued supplements, it's probably necessary.
If the purpose of the EE ban was to make new and interesting imbued
decks pop out of the woodwork (without, at a minimum, some chunk of
additional crypt options): Epic Fail.

witness1

Forcing players to make decisions is a good thing in my book.

> making the various Imbued decks look a lot more alike to one another.

> which attempt to use differing kinds of powers to win the game" - in
> the game, post-Edge-Explosion.

The 'significantly' part, I think, has already been established as the
part I'm not really willing to subscribe to, but... I guess we'll need
to wait and see.

Powers that (help a lot to) win the game? Vigilance, Donate (whose
worth dropped a little post-EE, since it became a tad more expensive
to use very often), Discern, Champion. Maybe Hide. That's it. It was
like this before EE, and post-EE one of those powers will be less used
while the non-listed ones still remain worthless.

> That's only because the pool of worthwhile powers are too small to
> go separate directions with it - assuming that's true. Remove that
> point and it could very well have an effect on diversity.

This we don't dispute - it's just that I'm thinking about the here and
now, besides supporting the point that worthwhile Powers are few.
I'm totally in favor of new Powers alongside banning EE, seems like
the best solution to me.

> > I have 3 copies of EE and never used more than 2 in the same deck, and
> > that was only once. I played Imbued for months before I even *had* a
> > single copy of it, and my decks neither changed much after that nor
> > started to win more games.
>
> Interesting. One of the guys I played against who was quite successful
> with his Imbued deck here in Arizona basically said the same thing.
> He didn't believe losing Edge Explosion was going to make a great
> deal of difference either. I'll be interested to see if that's true.

That's my guess. Of course, I can be very wrong - especially
considering I'm not known for coming up with new amazing combos or
deckbuilding ideas or whatever. But right now, I see no indication of
this changing in the near future (that is, before new cards are
released).

> > That is precisely my point (and I'd like to point out that I've also
> > included some 'at least until we don't get new cards' warning). So
> > maybe it's not that much of a disagreement as it seems.
>
> Maybe not. I must say, I find your view of the importance of Edge
> Explosion overall to Imbued decks to be quite different than some of the
> other posters, e.g. Sorrow who seemed rather despondent about Imbued decks
> ever winning again (at least until Imbued get some new stuff).
> Fred

I know. Suffice to say I don't really share Sorrow's opinion on that
particular point. I'm more worried about EE making certain powers and
cards with a per-use cost, like Donate, or some that cost more than 1
Conviction, like Imprison, a little more worthwhile in the long run
(that is, considering the whole course of a game) since you'll get
spent Convictions back faster at some point (assuming you survive in
the table while EE doesn't come by). It was worth it to put some extra
Donates on a deck with enough Martyrdom around and not use most of
them until EE was out. Removing EE makes it less probable and
efficient. I couldn't care much about the extra Power effect, and
making Donate a little less playable won't make for more diversity, I
think, just less flexibility for the Imbued.

Fabio 'Sooner' Macedo
